title: FastAPI Async & Database Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on how FastAPI runs async def vs def endpoints, SQLAlchemy 2.0 async sessions, session-per-request dependencies, background tasks and lifespan events.

chapters.title: async def vs def Endpoints
points: async def endpoints run directly on the event loop; def endpoints are sent to a threadpool (anyio, 40 threads by default) so they do not block the loop
Rule of thumb: use async def only if everything you await is async-native; use plain def when calling blocking libraries (requests, psycopg2, time.sleep)
Comparison: async def = cheap concurrency, but one blocking call stalls ALL requests; def = isolated per request, limited by thread count
Example: async def with await asyncio.sleep(1) vs def with time.sleep(1) both stay responsive, but time.sleep inside async def freezes the server
Mistake: calling blocking code (requests.get, sync DB driver, CPU loops) inside async def; fix with def, run_in_threadpool or asyncio.to_thread

layout.note: request to event loop vs threadpool
blocking call in async def freezes everything
Interview Point: Why does a blocking call in async def hurt more than in def? What is the default threadpool size? When would you pick def over async def?

chapters.title: SQLAlchemy 2.0 Async Engine and Session
points: create_async_engine('postgresql+asyncpg://...') needs an async driver (asyncpg, aiosqlite); a sync driver URL fails
async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False) is the session factory; expire_on_commit=False stops attribute reloads after commit that would trigger illegal lazy IO
Queries use 2.0 style: result = await session.execute(select(User).where(User.id == 1)); user = result.scalar_one_or_none()
Writes: session.add(obj); await session.commit(); await session.refresh(obj) to reload server-generated fields
Mistake: lazy-loading a relationship in async raises MissingGreenlet; fix with selectinload()/joinedload() in the query or await session.run_sync / awaitable_attrs

layout.note: Interview Point: Why expire_on_commit=False? What causes MissingGreenlet? How do you eager load relationships in async?

chapters.title: Session per Request via Dependencies
points: Pattern: one AsyncSession per request, created in a dependency and closed when the request ends
get_db is an async generator: async with SessionLocal() as session: yield session; the code after yield runs as cleanup
Inject with db: Annotated[AsyncSession, Depends(get_db)]; the same session is reused for all sub-dependencies in one request (dependency cache)
Transactions: commit explicitly in the endpoint or service, or rollback in an except block of the dependency so failures do not leave dirty state
Mistake: a global shared session across requests (not concurrency safe) or sharing one session between asyncio.gather tasks

layout.note: request lifecycle: open, yield, handler, close
never share a session across requests or tasks
Interview Point: Why is the session created per request? How does yield cleanup work in dependencies? Is an AsyncSession safe across concurrent tasks?

chapters.title: Background Tasks
points: BackgroundTasks runs a function after the response is sent: background_tasks.add_task(send_email, to, body)
The task function can be def (runs in the threadpool) or async def (runs on the event loop); args are passed to add_task
Use for short fire-and-forget work (emails, logs); use Celery/ARQ/RQ for heavy, retried or durable jobs since BackgroundTasks die with the process and have no retries
Example: endpoint takes background_tasks: BackgroundTasks, adds a task, returns {'status':'queued'} immediately
Mistake: reusing the request's DB session inside the task; the dependency session is already closed, so open a new session inside the task

layout.note: open a fresh session in the task
Interview Point: When does a background task run? When is BackgroundTasks not enough? Why not reuse the request session?

chapters.title: Lifespan Events
points: lifespan is an @asynccontextmanager passed as FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan); code before yield runs at startup, after yield at shutdown
Typical startup work: create the async engine and sessionmaker, load ML models, open Redis or HTTP client pools; store on app.state
Shutdown work: await engine.dispose(), close clients and flush resources
Lifespan replaces the deprecated @app.on_event('startup') and 'shutdown' handlers; do not mix both styles
Mistake: creating the engine per request instead of once in lifespan, or forgetting engine.dispose() so connections leak on shutdown

layout.note: one engine per app, disposed on shutdown
Interview Point: Where does startup code go in modern FastAPI? Why is one engine shared per process? What replaced on_event?

chapters.title: FastAPI Async Cheat Sheet
points: Blocking code: use def, or asyncio.to_thread / run_in_threadpool inside async def
Engine: create_async_engine(url) once in lifespan; sessionmaker: async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False)
Dependency: async with SessionLocal() as s: yield s; inject via Annotated[AsyncSession, Depends(get_db)]
Fire-and-forget: BackgroundTasks.add_task(fn, args) with its own session; heavy jobs go to a queue
Startup/shutdown: lifespan asynccontextmanager, engine.dispose() after yield; eager-load with selectinload to avoid MissingGreenlet

layout.note: Interview Point: Which rule prevents the most production bugs? How would you debug a stalled event loop? How do you size the threadpool?
